components.note: 一 (a line, representing a target or standard) — 正 shows a foot arriving exactly at the right mark.
止 (foot, to stop) — arriving and stopping precisely at the target gives 正 its meaning of 'correct' or 'straight.'
巾 (cloth) — 常 originally referred to a long skirt or banner made of cloth, later coming to mean something 'usual' or 'ordinary.'
尚 (shàng) gives a hint of the sound — 常 is pronounced cháng, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 医生说检查结果都很正常。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng shuō jiǎnchá jiéguǒ dōu hěn zhèngcháng.
example.english: The doctor said the checkup results are all normal.
example.fact: 正常 literally combines 正 ("correct, upright") and 常 ("usual, constant") — something that is both "correct" and "usual" is, quite transparently, "normal."

components.note: 匕 (a kneeling person) — a mourner bowed down in grief.
歹 (skeletal remains) — the corpse being mourned, the source of 死's meaning 'to die, dead.'
亡 is traditionally read as a person enclosed within a coffin or hidden away — an early image behind its meaning 'to die, to be lost.'

example.hanzi: 这场车祸造成了三人死亡。
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng chēhuò zàochéng le sān rén sǐwáng.
example.english: This car accident caused three deaths.
example.fact: 死亡 is the neutral, clinical register for "death" used in news reports and statistics — in everyday conversation about a person’s passing, Chinese speakers usually reach instead for the softer, more respectful 去世 or 过世, since a bare 死 (or 死亡 applied to someone you know) can sound abrupt or even callous.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 终 originally referred to the end of a woven thread, extended to mean 'end, final'
冬 (dōng) gives a loose sound connection to 终's reading zhōng

example.hanzi: 经过八个小时的飞行,我们终于到了。
example.pinyin: Jīngguò bā gè xiǎoshí de fēixíng, wǒmen zhōngyú dào le.
example.english: After an eight-hour flight, we finally arrived.
example.fact: 终于 marks the end of a long wait or difficult process and usually carries a note of relief or emotional payoff — its more neutral cousin 最后 ("lastly, in the end") simply marks sequence, with no implication that the wait was hard-won.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拥 describes holding someone in your arms.
用 (yòng) gives a sound distantly related to yōng, having drifted apart over time.
月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.

example.hanzi: 她拥有十年的教学经验。
example.pinyin: Tā yōngyǒu shí nián de jiàoxué jīngyàn.
example.english: She has ten years of teaching experience.
example.fact: 拥有 is the more formal, "weightier" word for "to have" — reserved for significant or abstract possessions like wealth, rights, talent, or experience — while everyday, concrete belongings ("I have a pen") almost always just take the plain verb 有.

components.note: 又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'

example.hanzi: 我们周末要开一个派对。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zhōumò yào kāi yí gè pàiduì.
example.english: We're having a party this weekend.
example.fact: 派对 is a phonetic loanword transliterating English "party" — one of a small class of borrowed sound-alike words in Mandarin (alongside 咖啡 kāfēi "coffee") that carry no meaning from their individual characters, only borrowed sound.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
再 depicts something stacked again on top of a base line — repetition, or doing something 'once more,' is pictured by piling on an extra layer.

example.hanzi: 他不再相信她了。
example.pinyin: Tā bú zài xiāngxìn tā le.
example.english: He no longer believes her.
example.fact: 不再 always sits directly before the verb to negate an ongoing or future continuation ("no longer doing X") and is regularly closed off with a sentence-final 了 to mark the change of state — its cousin 没再 instead negates a repeated action that simply didn’t happen again in the past.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咖 is used in a word for something taken by mouth (coffee).
加 (jiā) gives a sound close to kā, sharing the same rhyme with a different initial.
口 (mouth) — 啡 is used in a word for something taken by mouth (coffee).
非 (fēi) gives the sound — an exact match with 啡.

example.hanzi: 我每天早上都喝一杯咖啡。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang dōu hē yì bēi kāfēi.
example.english: I drink a cup of coffee every morning.
example.fact: Like 派对, 咖啡 is a sound-borrowed loanword for "coffee" — both syllables were chosen purely to approximate the foreign sound, which is why 咖 and 啡 are found in almost no other common words, existing mainly to spell out this one borrowed term.

components.note: 阝 (mound/hill) — 阻 originally described a hill or ridge blocking one's path.
且 (qiě) gives a sound distantly related to zǔ, having drifted apart over time.
止 depicts a footprint, with toes at the top and the leg below — a simple picture of a foot, later extended to mean 'to stop.'

example.hanzi: 警察及时阻止了这场冲突。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá jíshí zǔzhǐ le zhè chǎng chōngtū.
example.english: The police stopped the conflict in time.
example.fact: 阻 (a hill blocking the way) and 止 (a stopped foot) both independently mean "to block, to stop" — 阻止 stacks two already near-synonymous roots into one reinforced verb, a common Chinese word-building strategy also seen in this deck’s 喜欢 and 应该.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.
豕 (pig/boar) — appears as part of 象's original full-body pictograph of an elephant, reusing a four-legged-animal shape; 象 itself depicts an elephant's trunk and ears above the body.

example.hanzi: 很难想象没有手机的生活。
example.pinyin: Hěn nán xiǎngxiàng méiyǒu shǒujī de shēnghuó.
example.english: It's hard to imagine life without a phone.
example.fact: 想象 is the standard mainland spelling for "to imagine" — don’t be thrown by the near-identical variant 想像, still seen in some Taiwan and Hong Kong publications, which swaps in 像 ("to resemble") for 象; both point to the same word, just standardized differently by region.

components.note: 冫 (ice) — 冷 relates to the cold of ice
令 (lìng) gives a sound close to 冷's reading lěng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
青 (blue-green, nature) — 静 relates to a calm stillness, like still water or clear skies
争 (zhēng) gives a sound distantly related to 静's reading jìng, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 遇到问题的时候,你要保持冷静。
example.pinyin: Yùdào wèntí de shíhou, nǐ yào bǎochí lěngjìng.
example.english: When you run into a problem, you need to stay calm.
example.fact: 冷 ("cold") plus 静 ("still, quiet") combine almost literally into "cold and still" — an emotional-temperature metaphor much like English "keep a cool head," just built from the character level up rather than as a fixed idiom.

components.note: 氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.hanzi: 这是解决问题的好方法。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì jiějué wèntí de hǎo fāngfǎ.
example.english: This is a good way to solve the problem.
example.fact: 方法 names a concrete technique or procedure for getting something done, distinct from its near-synonym 办法 which leans toward a solution or workaround for a specific problem — "有办法" ("I’ve got a way") is common and casual in speech, but "有方法" sounds noticeably stiffer.

components.note: Originally a drawing of a bear, with 厶 as its head, ⺼ as its body, and 匕匕 as its claws; the picture was later borrowed to mean 'ability, to be able to.'
力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.

example.hanzi: 他的语言能力很强。
example.pinyin: Tā de yǔyán nénglì hěn qiáng.
example.english: His language ability is very strong.
example.fact: 能 (from an old pictograph of a bear, prized for its strength) plus 力 (from a plow blade, standing for physical effort) combine into "capacity for strength" — a fittingly muscular etymology for the modern, abstract word for "ability."

components.note: 宀 (roof/house) — relates to 完's meaning 'complete, finish,' as in a fully built house.
元 (yuán) was the phonetic base; the pronunciation later shifted to wán, so only a partial rhyme remains today.
羊 (sheep; here representing feathers or ornaments on a headdress) — an elaborate decoration worn on the head.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — a person wearing a decorated headdress was seen as beautiful, giving 美 its meaning 'beautiful.'

example.hanzi: 没有人是完美的。
example.pinyin: Méiyǒu rén shì wánměi de.
example.english: Nobody is perfect.
example.fact: 完 ("complete, finished") and 美 ("beautiful") combine into "completely beautiful" — a vivid, almost poetic image for what English flattens into the single abstract word "perfect."

components.note: 目 depicts an eye turned on its side, with the outline and pupil visible — later straightened into today's rectangular shape.
木 (wood/tree) — 标 originally referred to the tip of a tree, later coming to mean 'mark, sign'
票 (piào) gives a sound close to 标's reading biāo

example.hanzi: 我今年的目标是学会开车。
example.pinyin: Wǒ jīnnián de mùbiāo shì xuéhuì kāichē.
example.english: My goal this year is to learn to drive.
example.fact: 目 (eye) plus 标 (a marked tip or sign, originally the tip of a tree) combine into "what the eye is aimed at" — literally an archer’s point of aim, which is why 目标 covers both a literal physical target and an abstract life goal.

meanings: to have sth to do with

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.

example.hanzi: 这本书跟中国历史有关。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū gēn Zhōngguó lìshǐ yǒuguān.
example.english: This book is related to Chinese history.
example.fact: 有关 can either follow a noun with 跟/与 ("X 跟 Y 有关", "X is related to Y") or sit in front of a noun as a compact attributive ("有关部门", "the relevant department") — two distinct grammatical slots for the same two characters that learners often only pick up one of.

components.note: 米 (grain, especially husked rice) — 精's meaning 'refined, essence, spirit' relates to rice refined to its purest form.
青 (qīng) gives a sound hint — 精 is pronounced jīng, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant differs.
礻 (an altar, related to ritual/spirits) — 神 relates to gods and spirits.
申 (shēn) gives a hint of the sound — 神 is pronounced shén, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 老人的精神状态很好。
example.pinyin: Lǎorén de jīngshén zhuàngtài hěn hǎo.
example.english: The elderly person's mental state is very good.
example.fact: Written identically, 精神 also has a second, differently-toned reading recorded in some dictionaries — jīngshen, with a neutral second syllable — meaning "energetic, full of pep" (他看起来很精神, "he looks lively"), distinct from the fully-toned jīngshén used here for the noun senses "spirit, mind, consciousness."

components.note: 夕 (evening, night) — divination was traditionally done in the evening.
卜 (to divine, reading cracks in bone or shell) — combined with 夕 (evening), an evening divination was for unusual or 'outside' matters, giving 外 its meaning of 'outside' or 'foreign.'

example.hanzi: 我买了一本书,另外还买了一支笔。
example.pinyin: Wǒ mǎi le yì běn shū, lìngwài hái mǎi le yì zhī bǐ.
example.english: I bought a book, and besides that I also bought a pen.
example.fact: 另外 works both as a stand-alone connective adverb ("besides, in addition," linking two clauses) and as an attributive right before a noun meaning "another, a separate" (另外一个问题, "another problem") — two overlapping but distinct jobs bundled into one word.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with an implement, action) — relates to 放's meaning 'to let go, release, put.'
方 (fāng) gives the sound — 放 is pronounced fàng, a close match sharing the same rhyme.
木 (tree) — 松 names a type of tree, the pine.
公 (gōng) gives a rhyme close to sōng, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 周末我喜欢在家放松一下。
example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒ xǐhuan zài jiā fàngsōng yíxià.
example.english: On weekends I like to relax at home for a bit.
example.fact: 放 ("to release, let go") and 松 ("loose, slack" — the same character that names the pine tree) combine into "release and loosen," a physical image of untensing muscles that maps neatly onto the modern sense "to relax."

components.note: 亻 (person) leans to the side.
木 (tree) — a person resting against a tree gave 休 its meaning 'to rest.'
自 (nose) — the breath passing through.
心 (heart) — the breath of life, giving 息 its meaning 'to breathe; to rest; news.'

example.hanzi: 你工作太累了,应该休息一下。
example.pinyin: Nǐ gōngzuò tài lèi le, yīnggāi xiūxi yíxià.
example.english: You've been working too hard, you should rest a bit.
example.fact: 休 pictures a person 亻 leaning against a tree 木, and 息 combines 自 (nose) and 心 (heart) to depict the breath of life — 休息 pairs the image of "leaning to rest" with "catching one’s breath" into the everyday word for taking a break.

components.note: 母 (mǔ, 'mother') serves as the phonetic base; the sound has since diverged from měi, so the connection is mostly historical today.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'

example.hanzi: 我每天都去公园跑步。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān dōu qù gōngyuán pǎobù.
example.english: I go jogging in the park every day.
example.fact: 每 ("every") almost always pairs with 都 later in the sentence to reinforce its all-inclusive meaning — dropping 都 after 每天 isn’t technically wrong, but native speakers rarely do, since the pairing is close to a fixed habit of speech.

components.note: 回 depicts a spiral or winding shape — something that turns back on itself, giving rise to the meaning 'to return.'

example.hanzi: 请回答我的问题。
example.pinyin: Qǐng huídá wǒ de wèntí.
example.english: Please answer my question.
example.fact: 回答 is reserved for answering a question or responding to something specifically asked — it isn’t interchangeable with 回复 (huífù), the word for replying to a message, letter, or email, even though both can be rendered as "reply" in English.

components.note: 凵 depicts an open container or pit, shown here holding something dangerous inside.
乂 is a crossed mark suggesting something tangled or harmful — trapped inside the container 凵, it gives 凶 its meaning 'vicious, ominous.'
手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.

example.hanzi: 警察还没有找到凶手。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá hái méiyǒu zhǎodào xiōngshǒu.
example.english: The police still haven't found the murderer.
example.fact: 凶 ("vicious, ominous" — pictured as something dangerous trapped in a pit) plus 手 ("hand," here meaning "the one who does it," as in 打手 "hired thug" or 选手 "competitor") combine into "the vicious hand" — the literal image behind the word for a murderer.

components.note: 人 — a person, shown bending over
贝 (money/shell) — a heavy load of money the person is carrying on their back
责 shows 贝 (money, a cowry shell) at its base, tied to a debt that must be repaid — giving 责 its meaning 'duty, responsibility, to blame.'

example.hanzi: 谁负责这个项目?
example.pinyin: Shéi fùzé zhège xiàngmù?
example.english: Who is in charge of this project?
example.fact: 负责 works as a plain verb taking an object (负责这个项目, "to be in charge of this project") but also shifts into an adjective describing a personality trait (他很负责, "he’s very conscientious") — the same two characters covering both a job description and a character trait.

components.note: 人 (person) forms the top of the character.
八, shown here as a dividing line, suggests separation or a boundary — together with 人 above, giving 介 its meaning 'to lie between, to introduce.'
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.hanzi: 你介意我开窗吗?
example.pinyin: Nǐ jièyì wǒ kāichuāng ma?
example.english: Do you mind if I open the window?
example.fact: 介意 shows up almost exclusively in questions and negative sentences (你介意吗? "do you mind?"; 我不介意 "I don’t mind") — using it in a flat positive statement ("我介意", "I do mind") is grammatical but sounds unusually blunt and confrontational in everyday speech.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 试 relates to proposing or trying something out
式 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 试's pronunciation shì
讠 (speech) — 试 relates to proposing or trying something out
式 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 试's pronunciation shì

example.hanzi: 你要不要试试这个新餐厅?
example.pinyin: Nǐ yào bu yào shìshi zhège xīn cāntīng?
example.english: Do you want to try this new restaurant?
example.fact: 试试 is simply the verb 试 ("to try, to test") reduplicated — a common pattern also seen in 看看 ("take a look") and 想想 ("think it over") that softens a suggestion, making it sound more casual and tentative than the single-syllable 试 alone.

components.note: 大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'

example.hanzi: 我永远不会忘记那天。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒngyuǎn bú huì wàngjì nàtiān.
example.english: I will never forget that day.
example.fact: 那天 pins a memory or story to a specific, already-established day ("that day [we talked about]") — it needs shared context to refer back to, unlike 有一天 ("one day"), which introduces a brand-new, previously unmentioned day at the start of a narrative.

components.note: 糸 (thread/silk) — 系 relates to connecting or tying things together, like threads linking into a system.
纟 (thread) — 统 relates to threads gathered into one continuous strand, extending to the idea of unifying or governing as one system.
充 (chōng) gives a hint of the sound — 统 is pronounced tǒng, a connection that has shifted somewhat.

example.hanzi: 这个系统出了一些问题。
example.pinyin: Zhège xìtǒng chū le yìxiē wèntí.
example.english: This system has some problems.
example.fact: 系 (originally silk threads linking together) and 统 (threads gathered into one continuous strand) both independently evoke things tied into a whole — 系统 layers two "connected-threads" images into the modern abstract word for an organized, interconnected system.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 睡 relates to closing the eyes to sleep.
垂 (chuí) gives a sound partly close to shuì, sharing part of the rhyme.
见 (to see, perceive) — relates to 觉's meaning 'to feel, sense, perceive.'
⺍ is a small graphic element serving as the phonetic hint, though its link to jué's modern sound has faded after centuries of change.

example.hanzi: 我每天十一点睡觉。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān shíyī diǎn shuìjiào.
example.english: I go to sleep at eleven every day.
example.fact: 睡觉 looks like a fused single verb but is actually a verb-object compound that other elements can split apart — 睡了一觉 ("slept a sleep," i.e. "took a nap") and 睡午觉 ("take a midday nap") both insert material between 睡 and 觉, something a true single verb could never allow.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谋 relates to discussing and forming a plan.
某 (mǒu) gives the sound — an exact match with 谋.
乂 depicts crossed strokes suggesting a cutting action.
木 (wood) here represents a wooden stake — giving 杀 its meaning 'to kill.'

example.hanzi: 警方怀疑这是一起谋杀案。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng huáiyí zhè shì yì qǐ móushā àn.
example.english: The police suspect this is a murder case.
example.fact: 谋杀 specifically implies premeditation — the 谋 half literally means "to plot, to scheme" — distinguishing it from the broader 杀 ("to kill") or 杀人 ("to kill a person"), which make no claim about whether the killing was planned in advance.

components.note: 礻 (spirit, altar) — 礼 relates to ceremony and rites performed before the spirits.
乚 reflects the character's phonetic root, though its exact link to the modern reading lǐ is unclear today.
牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这是我送给你的礼物。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ sòng gěi nǐ de lǐwù.
example.english: This is the gift I’m giving you.
example.fact: 礼 (rooted in 礻, an altar — its core sense is "ritual, ceremony") plus 物 ("object, thing") combine into "a ceremonial object" — a formal origin for the now-casual word for any gift, tracing back to the offerings exchanged during ancient rites.

components.note: 禾 (grain/rice plant) — 种 relates to seeds and planting crops.
中 (zhōng) gives the sound — 种 is pronounced zhǒng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 我不喜欢那种电影。
example.pinyin: Wǒ bù xǐhuan nà zhǒng diànyǐng.
example.english: I don't like that kind of movie.
example.fact: 那种 always needs a noun to follow it (那种电影, "that kind of movie") — for a stand-alone "that kind" without naming the noun, Chinese switches to 那样 ("like that") instead, since 种 is functioning here as a measure word, and measure words don’t usually stand alone without the noun they count.

components.note: 夂 (a foot, to walk) — 各 pictures people arriving from different directions.
口 (mouth) — different people speaking gave 各 its meaning 'each' or 'every,' emphasizing individual distinctness.
亻 (person) — 位 relates to a person's location.
立 (to stand) — the spot where a person stands gave 位 its meaning 'position' or 'place,' and later, a polite measure word for people.

example.hanzi: 各位好,欢迎来到我们公司。
example.pinyin: Gèwèi hǎo, huānyíng lái dào wǒmen gōngsī.
example.english: Hello everyone, welcome to our company.
example.fact: 各位 is a polite, slightly formal way to address a group — the natural choice for opening a speech, meeting, or announcement — while the more casual 大家 ("everybody") is the default among friends or in everyday conversation.

components.note: 钅 (metal/gold) — represents something valuable.
昔 (formerly, in the past) — valuable metal that has been mishandled or lost over time gave 错 its meaning 'mistake, wrong.'
讠 (speech) — 误 began as a mistake in speech, later broadening to 'error' in general.
吴 (wú) gives a sound close to wù, with the tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 每个人都会犯错误。
example.pinyin: Měi gèrén dōu huì fàn cuòwù.
example.english: Everyone makes mistakes.
example.fact: 错 (originally describing tarnished, mishandled metal) and 误 (originally a mistake made in speech) both independently mean "wrong, mistaken" — 错误 combines two near-synonymous "wrong" roots into one reinforced noun, the same doubling pattern seen in 喜欢 and 应该 elsewhere in this deck.

components.note: 阝 (a mound/city) — represents a place being traveled to.
迶 depicts walking or moving along a path — following someone to the city gave 随 its meaning 'to follow, along with.'

example.hanzi: 你随便坐,不用客气。
example.pinyin: Nǐ suíbiàn zuò, bú yòng kèqi.
example.english: Sit wherever you like, no need to be so polite.
example.fact: 随便 shifts easily between a relaxed, positive sense ("as you please, whatever works," 随便你 "however you like") and a mildly critical one ("careless, sloppy," 太随便了 "way too careless") — tone of voice and context, not the word itself, decide which reading applies.

components.note: 大 (big) — in 头's simplified form, this element is linked to the idea of 'high' or topmost, since the head sits at the top of the body.

example.hanzi: 她的头发很长。
example.pinyin: Tā de tóufa hěn cháng.
example.english: Her hair is very long.
example.fact: 头发 refers only to the hair on one’s head — body hair, animal fur, and plant fuzz all take the separate word 毛 instead, so "他有很多头发" strictly means "he has a lot of hair on his head," not hair in general.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.hanzi: 父母一直很关心我的学习。
example.pinyin: Fùmǔ yìzhí hěn guānxīn wǒ de xuéxí.
example.english: My parents have always cared a lot about my studies.
example.fact: 关心 expresses caring through personal attention to someone’s wellbeing (关心某人, "to care about someone"), distinct from 关注 (guānzhù), which means to follow or pay attention to an issue, topic, or public figure without necessarily implying personal warmth.

meanings: variant of 幹嘛|干嘛[gan4 ma2]

components.note: A pictograph of an ancient forked weapon, such as a club or shield-tipped spear — the tool image later extended to 干's meanings 'to do, to work' and, in another reading, 'dry.'
口 (mouth) — relates to 吗's role as a spoken question particle.
马 (mǎ) provides the base sound, though 吗 is usually spoken with a neutral, unstressed tone.

example.hanzi: 你干吗不早点告诉我?
example.pinyin: Nǐ gànmá bù zǎodiǎn gàosu wǒ?
example.english: Why didn't you tell me sooner?
example.fact: 干 is one of Chinese’s classic reading-switchers — pronounced gān it means "dry," but here, meaning "to do" (as in 干嘛/干吗, "to do what"), it’s read gàn; the two senses, merged into one simplified character today, trace back to separate traditional characters (乾 and 幹).

meanings: interest (thing in which one is interested)

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) — 趣 originally related to hurrying eagerly toward something, extending to 'interesting, of interest.'
取 (qǔ) gives a sound close to qù, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.

example.hanzi: 他对音乐很感兴趣。
example.pinyin: Tā duì yīnyuè hěn gǎn xìngqù.
example.english: He's very interested in music.
example.fact: 兴趣 as a noun almost always appears inside the fixed frame "对...感兴趣" ("to feel interest toward...") — learners who try to use it as a plain verb the way English uses "to interest" often produce sentences that sound slightly off; the noun-plus-感 construction is the reliable default.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 报 relates to taking action against someone.
卩 (a kneeling or bound person) — handling a wrongdoer and announcing the judgment gave 报 its meaning 'to report' or 'to announce.'
口 (mouth) — the act of speaking.
牛 (ox) — traditionally read as speaking with the forceful weight of an ox, giving 告 its meaning 'to tell, announce, inform.'

example.hanzi: 我明天要交一份报告。
example.pinyin: Wǒ míngtiān yào jiāo yí fèn bàogào.
example.english: I have to hand in a report tomorrow.
example.fact: 报 (a hand 扌 subduing a bound wrongdoer 卩 to announce a judgment) and 告 (mouth 口 plus ox 牛, "to speak with force") both independently carry a sense of "to announce, to inform" — 报告 doubles up two announcing-roots into the modern word for a formal report.

components.note: 人 (person), doubled — one person shown following another depicts the idea of accompanying or coming from somewhere.
氵 (water) — 没 originally meant to sink or drown in water, later extended to the negative 'not have.'
殳 (shū) is the historical sound component; it no longer rhymes with méi in modern Mandarin, another case of sound drift over time.

example.hanzi: 我从没去过西藏。
example.pinyin: Wǒ cóngméi qùguò Xīzàng.
example.english: I've never been to Tibet.
example.fact: 从没 is short for 从来没(有) and is almost always followed by a verb marked with the experiential 过 (从没...过, "have never ever...") — dropping 过 in a 从没 sentence about past experience usually sounds incomplete to native ears, since 过 is what signals "at any point up to now."

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.
厤 (relating to the sequence of time) — 历 relates to history and the calendar
力 (lì) gives the sound — 历 is pronounced lì, an exact match

example.hanzi: 这是我人生中一次难忘的经历。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ rénshēng zhōng yí cì nánwàng de jīnglì.
example.english: This is an unforgettable experience in my life.
example.fact: 经历 names something a person personally lived through, usually over time (a hardship, a journey, a career) — its near-synonym 经验 (jīngyàn) instead names the practical know-how gained from doing something repeatedly, so a single dramatic event is an 经历, while years of practice building skill is 经验.

components.note: 耂 (a person bent with age, with long hair) — depicts an elderly figure.
匕 (here representing a cane or walking stick) — combined with the bent figure above, 老 pictures an old person leaning on a cane.
帀 (a banner or covering) — flying above the scene.
刂 (a knife) — wielded with skill beneath the banner, an image of expertise giving 师 its meaning 'master, teacher, expert.'

example.hanzi: 我们的老师非常认真。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen de lǎoshī fēicháng rènzhēn.
example.english: Our teacher is extremely conscientious.
example.fact: 老师 has increasingly become a generic polite address term even outside the classroom — waitstaff, strangers giving directions, or hosts on a talk show may all be addressed as 老师 as a mark of respect for perceived expertise, not because they are literally anyone’s teacher.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'

example.hanzi: 不用担心,一切都会好的。
example.pinyin: Bú yòng dānxīn, yíqiè dōu huì hǎo de.
example.english: Don't worry, everything will be fine.
example.fact: 不用 politely waves something off as unnecessary ("no need to...") — softer than the flat negative command 不要 ("don’t...") — so being offered tea and answering 不用,谢谢 ("no need, thanks") comes across far gentler than a blunt 不要.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
子 (child) — 孩 relates directly to children
亥 (hài) gives a sound close to 孩's reading hái

example.hanzi: 那个小孩在公园里玩。
example.pinyin: Nàge xiǎohái zài gōngyuán lǐ wán.
example.english: That child is playing in the park.
example.fact: 小孩 is the everyday, spoken-register word for "child" — its close relative 孩子 is more neutral and comfortable in both speech and writing, while 小孩(儿) leans distinctly casual and conversational.

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 人类是唯一会使用复杂语言的动物。
example.pinyin: Rénlèi shì wéiyī huì shǐyòng fùzá yǔyán de dòngwù.
example.english: Humans are the only animals that use complex language.
example.fact: 类 means "category, kind," so 人类 is literally "the human category" — a species-level term reserved for humanity as a whole, distinct from 人们 ("people," a plural group of individuals) or a single 人 ("a person").

components.note: A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'
由 resembles 田 (a field) with a stem or road extending from it — pointing the way toward a source, which gave 由 its meaning of 'from' or 'cause.'

example.hanzi: 每个人都应该享有自由。
example.pinyin: Měi gè rén dōu yīnggāi xiǎngyǒu zìyóu.
example.english: Everyone should be entitled to freedom.
example.fact: 由 on its own already carries the sense "from, cause" (as in 由于, "due to") — 自由 combines it with 自 ("self") into "arising from oneself," a literal image of self-determination that happens to parallel the Greek roots of English "autonomy" (autos "self" + nomos "law").

components.note: 又 (a hand) — reaching out for support.
十 (a branch) — held in the hand, the image of support giving 支 its meaning 'to support, prop up; branch.'
扌 (hand) — relates directly to 持's meaning 'to hold, maintain.'
寺 (sì) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from chí.

example.hanzi: 谢谢大家一直支持我。
example.pinyin: Xièxie dàjiā yìzhí zhīchí wǒ.
example.english: Thank you all for always supporting me.
example.fact: 支 (a hand holding a branch, "to prop up") and 持 (a hand holding something steady, "to maintain") both independently involve a hand keeping something upright — 支持 combines two "steadying hand" images into the abstract modern sense of supporting a person, cause, or opinion.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 星 relates to bright heavenly bodies like the sun and stars
生 (shēng) gives a sound close to 星's reading xīng
月 (moon) — 期 relates to time measured by the moon's cycles, like a period or term.
其 (qí) gives a hint of the sound — 期 is pronounced qī, a connection that has shifted slightly in tone.

example.hanzi: 这个星期我很忙。
example.pinyin: Zhège xīngqī wǒ hěn máng.
example.english: I'm very busy this week.
example.fact: 星期 names the seven-day week itself (这个星期, "this week") but, attached to a number, also names a single day within it (星期一, literally "week-one," i.e. Monday) — one word doing double duty as both the container and its individual slices, unlike English’s separate "week" and "Monday."

components.note: 彳 (step, to walk) — an older, now faded connection tied to movement.
艮 (gèn) gives a hint of the sound — 很 is pronounced hěn, a connection that has drifted significantly over time.
忄 (heart/mind) — the state of mind being described.
夬 (a decisive, resolute action) — a resolute state of mind, giving 快 its meaning 'fast, quick.'

example.hanzi: 他很快就回来了。
example.pinyin: Tā hěn kuài jiù huílái le.
example.english: He came back very quickly.
example.fact: 很快 can describe the manner of an action (跑得很快, "runs very fast") or, placed at the front of a clause, shift to mean "soon" about a near-future event (很快就要下雨了, "it’s going to rain very soon") — the same two characters covering both a speed and a near-future timeframe.

components.note: 屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.
气 (simplified from 氣) depicts rising wisps or vapor, like breath or steam drifting upward — a simple picture of air or gas.

example.hanzi: 别生气了,这不是什么大事。
example.pinyin: Bié shēngqì le, zhè bú shì shénme dà shì.
example.english: Don't be angry, this isn't a big deal.
example.fact: 生 ("to arise, to be born") plus 气 ("qi, vital energy") combine into "energy arising" — the same 气 that names the vital life-force in traditional medicine and tai chi, here channeled specifically into the rising heat of anger.
